P1.evidence: Application acknowledged but not read back to make him feel seen — "I do know that you filled in an application, but I would just like to do it the old-fashioned way", and later "I thought that when I was quickly looking over your application." Three-part frame only: "get to know you, get to hear where you're currently at, where you want to go. See if we can help you bridge that gap" — no 'what's in the way' or 'what you need'. Agreement taken and the open question run cleanly.

P2.evidence: The injury screen was the strongest part of the baseline and was pushed properly — shoulder duration, the L5 injury at 14, and the ankle were each followed up ("Is your lower back also tight at the moment or is your lower back more on the pain side?"). Diet was walked meal by meal. Energy was explored and became the emotional centre of the call. Against that: the prospect's occupation was never asked and is still unknown at the end of a 52-minute call, health conditions were never asked as a category, sleep was never asked even though the prospect raised it himself ("it depends on what I eat, on how much I sleep"), and age, height and weight all arrived because he volunteered them or they were on the form. Training frequency was never established — only that sessions are 25-30 minutes.

P3.evidence: Good surface work and a genuinely excellent reflect-back at 00:26:27 that ran the whole picture back including the uncomfortable part ("Nutrition, to be honest, it's quite all over the place"). The bridge past the physical was run twice and produced the real driver: "it's for my mental health, you know. I want to feel good." But the depth stopped there. 'Who else does that impact' was never asked — no partner, family, children or anyone else entered the conversation despite weekly family dinners being mentioned — and the drive to legacy or identity got only as far as "a better version of myself" and the biological clock. The specific physical thing he cannot do (run, touch the floor) was volunteered, not asked for.

P4.evidence: Best-run phase. Past attempt asked directly — "What made you stop with that and then be like, okay, I actually want to do something with kettlebells?" — producing the full three-year history with the personal trainer, why it went digital (cost) and how it ended ("he flew to Thailand... and he kind of forgot about me"). The rep landed the structural read out loud: "Okay, sounds like you always need someone to push you." The gap question was asked as written — "what is missing for you, Nadav, at the moment that we need to help you solve specifically?" — and he named it himself. The self-reliance challenge ("why can't you stick to it on your own?") was never put.

P5.evidence: Consequence question asked properly — "if you don't set a step for yourself, where do you think that you would be in a year from now, if you don't really make those changes that you know that you need to make?" — and the answer was weak ("maybe a couple of steps further, but not in the place that I really want to be"). Settle check run and produced the one moment of real energy in the call: "No, no. I want the whole thing." The rep then moved straight to praise rather than pressing 'why not', and no line in the sand was asked for.

P6.evidence: Correctly sequenced — the commitment check ran at 00:31:54, before the presentation began at 00:33:13: "Do you feel like there would be any reason why you're not going to be able to succeed?" / "No." A second belief check was run again before price at 00:42:26 and pressed for the reason behind the yes ("what's the part that's telling you, yeah, that's going to work?"), which is better than the script asks for. Scored partial on P6b only because the question asked about ability to succeed rather than willingness to go all in — the go-all-in framing is what would have surfaced the budget before the offer rather than after it.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted but the prospect declined both tiers on affordability ("at the moment, I cannot afford it", "it's not what I'm looking at right now"), so payment and onboarding were never reachable. No payment, no Trevor booking, no agreement, no welcome instructions — correctly, because there was no sale.

objection_plays.detail: Isolation ran cleanly ("outside of the investment, so sort of setting that aside for a second, do you feel like, yeah, I want to start with this?") and the rep correctly distinguished can't-afford from not-worth-it ("is it more of a case of like, I just don't have that in my bank account at the moment, or is it more so like, I don't feel like it's worth that 6k?"). Two financial-picture questions ran — month-end surplus and savings. Then it stopped: no credit cards, no available credit, no used-versus-available, no crypto or investments, no "most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up", no "you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place". Given the prospect disclosed zero savings and month-to-month living, stopping is defensible — but the play was not run, it was abandoned in favour of a cheaper product.
"I'm going to have to think about it" landed at 00:49:55 on the downsell and no move was made against it. The rep answered the follow-up price question and let it stand.

Trigger was explicit — "Maybe in a couple of months, you know, when I see my bank was letting me... Save some and focus on the budget." The rep agreed immediately and booked a check-in. None of the OD moves ran. In this specific case the objection is genuine cashflow rather than avoidance, so running the play hard would have been the wrong call — but the script offers no alternative, which is the finding.

Script gap, clinical. The prospect disclosed a named chronic bone condition (Müller-Weiss disease in the left ankle, running impossible), an L5 spinal injury and four years of undiagnosed shoulder pain. There is no scripted path for this. The rep improvised twice — an absolute safety promise in the presentation ("he's going to teach you how all the movement actually works. So you're not going to be able to hurt yourself") and a dismissal when pitching the self-directed tier ("you don't even actually really have injuries at the moment, more so stiffnesses"). Neither is in the playbook, and nothing in the playbook tells him to ask about clinical clearance.

Script gap, prior-coach anchor. The prospect had three years with a personal trainer that produced results and ended because of cost and abandonment, not because it failed. Objection C assumes capacity to pay is the blocker; here the blocker was a working cheaper substitute plus genuine poverty. The rep differentiated on duration and teaching ("we're not personal trainers... you're going to be with us for six months, probably. And then that's it") which is the right instinct, but there is no scripted play behind it.

notes: Structurally the best-sequenced call of the batch — commitment check before the presentation, a real reflect-back, and past attempts asked directly — and it still lost, correctly, to a prospect with no savings in a high-inflation economy. Two coaching points that are independent of the outcome: the occupation was never asked, so affordability was unknowable until the number landed 44 minutes in; and 'who else does this impact' was skipped entirely, which is where the emotional weight for a 36-year-old with family dinners every Friday was sitting. The serious issue is not adherence but the two improvised clinical reassurances.
